thread.title: Moustapha Thiam adjusting to enhanced offensive role
thread.title_full: Moustapha Thiam adjusting to enhanced offensive role

author: Suraj Kodali
title: Moustapha Thiam adjusting to enhanced offensive role
text:
Upon transferring to the Michigan men’s basketball team, junior center Moustapha Thiam was lauded for his size and athleticism that could stabilize the defense of a new-look frontcourt.
Thiam’s offensive flashes, however, have been the most eye-catching early on this season. It’s reflected in not only the numbers he’s putting up, but also in how often Wolverines coach Mike Boynton Jr. is deploying him.
“I would just say I’m more involved,” Thiam said Thursday at Michigan Media Day. “They’re playing through me and (senior forward J.P. Estrella) a lot.”
After a strong season at Cincinnati, Thiam’s offensive ability couldn’t be undermined. His 12.8 points per game was a key draw as one of the most attractive prospects in the portal, on top of his capacity to shoot the 3-pointer. But the majority of damage Thiam did on the offensive end was typical of the average 7-foot-2 center, relying on his size and prowess as a rim runner.
It took no time at all for Michigan to see that aspect of his game, scoring immediately off the tip-off against Eastern Michigan on a lob from senior guard Elliot Cadeau. Thiam has already showcased the havoc he can wreak operating in the low post. Not only is he scoring from the field, but he’s drawing fouls at a high rate, shooting 18 free throws in the Wolverines’ first two exhibitions.
But Thiam isn’t only being utilized in the dunker spot. An early development from preseason is Boynton’s use of Thiam as an offensive hub, allowing him to operate as a passer from the nail alongside Cadeau and sophomore guard Trey McKenney. Returns on this strategy have been encouraging, with Thiam recording eight assists and just two turnovers.
“(Thiam) is playing in a system like this for the first time where he’s being asked to be a decision maker and be a hub, but the skill set is there to do it,” Boynton said Friday. “With more reps, it’ll become more natural to him.”
For someone who averaged just 0.5 assists per game last season, Thiam’s feel and chemistry with his teammates in these actions are notable. Whether it’s off-ball as a screener or creating on-ball, Thiam has looked in sync, especially with his backcourt duo.
“Me and (Cadeau) have tried to be more conscious of being closer to (Thiam),” McKenney said Thursday at Michigan Media Day. “I think we’ve done a good job of just making him more comfortable and him making us more comfortable.”
However, Boynton will also want Thiam far away from McKenney at times. The spacing that he provides for someone at his size is unique, which should give Michigan’s ball handlers more room to work. But in order for that to be the case, opposing teams must respect Thiam as a shooter.
Thiam averaged an attempted 1.6 3-pointers per game last season, converting 28.8% of them. While the occasional threat was there, the Wolverines will hope that aspect of his game takes a leap this year. Thiam attempted six 3-pointers against Oregon State, a sign of his greater emphasis toward using the long ball.
“We’re very comfortable with (Thiam) shooting a 3-pointer late,” Boynton said Oct. 11. “Most of the time, he’s going to rather that than his mid-range turnaround.”
A 7-foot-2 center affecting the game from different levels is a welcome sign for Michigan. If Thiam’s preseason shooting, passing and free-throw rate can translate to regular season action, he could be primed for a breakout campaign.
